Here, neglecting small corrections due to Z0 not being zero (Methods), the displacements δZ and \(\delta Y\approx \sin \delta \phi \approx \delta \phi \) evolve under the effective Lagrangian density.

Recent findings suggest that the energy cost of a ϕ displacement is only due to U ∝ ħΩ, but the cost of a Z displacement also includes an interaction-energy penalty, ∝ μs. The ratio of these costs gives the ratio of the oscillation amplitudes:.

and their product gives the plasma-oscillation frequency.

In the non-interacting (Rabi) limit AZ = AY and ωp = Ω, and in the Josephson regime AZ ≪ AY, which is essential for the implementation of the sine-Gordon model, and \(\hbar {\omega }_{{\rm{p}}}\approx \sqrt{2\hbar \varOmega {\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}}\gg \hbar \varOmega \) is the mass gap m*c2 in equation (1).

In a recent development, our measurements (Fig. 3c) agree with the predictions of equations (3) and (4) over three orders of magnitude in μs/(ħΩ). Crucially, we observe coherent oscillations deep in the Josephson regime, up to μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 102.

Sources indicate that next, we turn to the finite-momentum (k > 0) spin excitations (Fig. 4). By modulating Ω at frequency ωm, we parametrically excite finite-k spin modes with frequency ωs(k) = ωm/2 (Fig. 4a). It is noted that the coupling of this parametric drive to the total-density modes is much weaker. Figure 4b reveals example images with and without parametric modulation. We measure n−i(x, y), which reveals the ϕ excitations. For every ωm, we observe ϕ modulations with a well-defined spatial frequency k, and thus map out the spin dispersion relation, shown in Fig. 4c for different m* values.

a, Experimental protocol. We parametrically excite the system by modulating Ω at frequency ωm. The injected energy, in quanta of ħωm, is converted to pairs of spatial excitations with opposite momenta, each carrying energy ħωm/2. b, Example measurements. Top: after the parametric modulation, images of n−i show fluctuations with a characteristic ωm-dependent length scale. Scale bar, 20 μm. Bottom: normalizing the spatial power spectrum of the fluctuations observed with modulation to that without modulation, we reveal the dominant k excited at each ωm, which gives ωs(k) = ωm/2. Each data point is based on five independent experimental runs; the symbols show the mean values and the error bars denote the s.e.m. The solid lines show Gaussian fits. c, Dispersion relations for different field masses m*, tuned by varying the value of Ω (around which we modulate); here we also include k = 0 plasma-oscillation measurements. The solid lines show theoretical predictions from equation (5). The dashed lines indicate the inverse magnetic healing lengths \(1/{\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{2m\varOmega /\hbar }\); in our system, ξM corresponds to the reduced Compton wavelength ħ/(m*c). The dotted line reveals the inverse spin healing length, \(1/{\xi }_{{\rm{s}}}=\sqrt{2m{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/{\hbar }^{2}}\), which sets the low-k range where the dispersion is approximately relativistic (see text). The error bars in k denote the Gaussian widths of the spectra such as shown in b. For these measurements Z0 = 0.31.

The measured dispersion is in good agreement with the theoretical prediction5,19 (see also Methods).

where ϵk = ħ2k2/(2m). For k ≲ 1/ξs ≈ 2.6 μm−1, where \({\xi }_{{\rm{s}}}=\sqrt{{\hbar }^{2}/(2m{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})}\) is the spin healing length, this prediction is close to the massive relativistic dispersion relation.

where we now use the more general expressions for \(c\approx \sqrt{(\hbar \varOmega +{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})/m}\) and \({m}^{\ast }\approx m\sqrt{\hbar \varOmega (\hbar \varOmega +2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})/{(\hbar \varOmega +{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}})}^{2}}\), which are valid for any μs/(ħΩ); see Extended Data Fig. 1 for a comparison between equations (5) and (6).

For Ω = 0, the dispersion is gapless, while a non-zero Ω opens up a gap at k = 0 (see also ref. 38). For a massive relativistic field, the transition from the low-energy quadratic dispersion to the higher-energy linear dispersion is set by the reduced Compton wavelength ƛ = ħ/(m*c), which here corresponds to the magnetic (Rabi) healing length \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\). Our ability to tune \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/(\hbar \varOmega )={({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}/{\xi }_{{\rm{s}}})}^{2}\gg 1\) gives us a k range where the relativistic nature of the massive dispersion is notable.

Industry observers note that we now turn to exploring the non-perturbative sine-Gordon dynamics, by initializing the system at a large global phase displacement ϕ0 (Fig. 5a).

a, We study the dynamics following a large initial phase displacement ϕ0. For ∣ϕ0∣ < π, the plasma-oscillation period is ϕ0-dependent owing to the concavity of U(ϕ). For ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may eventually settle to different potential minima, which results in domain walls across which ϕ winds by 2π. b, Large-amplitude oscillations. Left: for different ϕ0, the system takes different time, τ, to return to ϕ = 0. Solid lines show sinusoidal fits; for large ϕ0, the oscillation is visibly anharmonic. Each data point is based on five independent experimental runs, and the error bars show the s.e.m. Right: τ/τ0 versus ϕ0; here τ0 = π/(2ωp) is the ϕ0-independent perturbative result. The solid line is the prediction based on the pendulum model. The errors in τ correspond to half of the spacing between the sampled t values. Here, Z0 = 0.31, Ω/(2π) = 74 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 11. c,d, Domain walls. The system is prepared at ϕ ≈ π at t = 0, and allowed to relax for 10 ms, corresponding to approximately 7τ0; here Z0 = 0.53, Ω/(2π) = 22 Hz and μs/(ħΩ) ≈ 39. Scale bar, 20 μm. In c, we show examples of domain walls seen in n+ and n− images, where they appear as, respectively, low- and high-density lines; each image shows an independent realization. In d, we show phase maps that reveal the 2π phase winding at domain walls. We interfere the two spin states using a pair of Raman–Bragg laser beams with wavevectors q1,2, and the imaged density distribution, nRB, shows modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\), where q = q1 − q2 and r = (x, y). From such fringe patterns we reconstruct the phase maps shown in the bottom panels (see text for details).

For ∣ϕ0∣ < π, we observe the anharmonic nature of the sine-Gordon potential, \(U(\phi )\propto -\cos (\phi )\), by measuring the time, τ, it takes the system to return from ϕ0 to ϕ = 0 (Fig. 5b). Here, we extract \(\phi =\arctan (Y/X)\), where Y and X are the separately measured projections of the global Bloch vector. In the perturbative regime, U(ϕ) is approximately harmonic and τ ≈ π/(2ωp) is independent of ϕ0. However, as ϕ0 → π, the concavity of U becomes increasingly relevant and τ grows, in analogy with a mechanical pendulum with a large initial angular displacement (solid line in Fig. 5b, right). At longer times these oscillations damp out, and this damping is accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures corresponding to k > 0 excitations (Extended Data Fig. 2).

Industry observers note that for ϕ0 = π, different regions of the system may settle into different potential minima, leading to the formation of domain walls across which ϕ rapidly winds by 2π. We observe such walls in most experimental realizations, with their spatial patterns varying randomly shot to shot (Fig. 5c,d).

In the images of n+ and n− (Fig. 5c), the walls appear as lines of low and high density, respectively. Here we show images from different experimental realizations, but note that if we image both n+ and n− in the same experimental run, we see that they are complementary (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Sources indicate that in Fig. 5d, we explicitly demonstrate the 2π phase winding across the domain walls. Here, just before imaging the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) component, we perform a fast (approximately 6 μs) π/2 spin rotation using a resonant two-photon Raman–Bragg coupling (see cartoon) instead of a radio-frequency field. Compared with the radio-frequency field that has a spatially uniform phase across the cloud, the Raman–Bragg coupling leads to a complex Ω with a spatially varying phase q ⋅ r; here r = (x, y) and q = q1 − q2, where q1,2 are the wavevectors of the two laser beams. In the Bloch-sphere picture, the Raman–Bragg Rabi vector always lies in the equatorial plane, but its orientation varies along the direction defined by q. Consequently, the imaged density nRB(x, y) demonstrates modulations \(\propto \cos ({\bf{q}}\cdot {\bf{r}}+\phi )\). For a spatially uniform ϕ, this is a pattern of straight parallel fringes with period 2π/q ≈ 2.51 μm, whereas spatial variations of ϕ(x, y) lead to fringe deformations. In particular, a domain wall perpendicular to q changes the fringe spacing, whereas a wall parallel to q shifts the fringe phase by 2π. In Fig. 5d, we show both  the straight fringes observed at t = 0 ms and two examples of domain walls observed after 10 ms of relaxation; the bottom panels show the reconstructed phase maps (see Extended Data Fig. 4 for more details).

The characteristic width, w, of an equilibrium domain wall is set by the competition between the potential energy per unit length, ∝ ħΩ ⋅ nw, and the corresponding kinetic energy, ∝ ħ2/(2mw2) ⋅ nw. Similarly to the oscillator length in a quantum harmonic oscillator, this competition gives w = ƛ = \({\xi }_{{\rm{M}}}=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

In Fig. 6a, we extract the domain-wall widths from both the n± images and the phase maps. In all cases, one-dimensional cuts perpendicular to the walls are fitted well by the theoretically predicted10 forms n±(z) = n0 ± n1sech2(z/w) and ϕ(z) = 4arctan[exp(z/w)]; here, z is the coordinate perpendicular to a wall centred at z = 0, and n0, n1 and w are fit parameters. The extracted values of w have a wide distribution (see histograms), probably because our domain walls are excited, but the three mean values are (within one standard deviation) consistent with each other and with the theoretically predicted w, indicated on the histograms by the dashed lines; it is noted that here we include an 8% correction to the predicted w due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods).

Recent findings suggest that a, For the experimental protocol as in Fig. 5, we extract the wall widths, w, from n+ and n− images, such as shown in Fig. 5c, and the phase maps, such as shown in Fig. 5d. We fit cuts perpendicular to the walls to the theoretically expected profiles (solid lines, see text). The histograms show width distributions based on >100 experimental images, and the dashed lines indicate the theoretically predicted w. b, The effect of changing Ω on the domain-wall width. Here the experimental protocol is the same, except that for the last 2 ms of relaxation we jump Ω/(2π) from 22 Hz to either 10 Hz or 45 Hz. The representative n+ images show an increase of the wall widths in the former case and decrease in the latter. Scale bar, 20 μm. The summary of the extracted mean widths is consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\). The dashed line demonstrates the theoretically predicted w, including an 8% correction due to our non-zero Z0 (Methods). The solid line shows the same trend with systematically 15% lower values. The error bars show the standard deviations of the w distributions. The different symbols corresponding to the same Ω are slightly offset horizontally for clarity.

In a recent development, finally, in Fig. 6b, we show that the characteristic wall width responds to changes in Ω. Here we initiate the system dynamics as in Fig. 5c, but quench Ω either down or up for the last 2 ms of relaxation. In the representative n+ images, one can see the systematic change in the wall widths, and the widths extracted as in Fig. 6a are consistent with the expected trend \(w\propto 1/\sqrt{\varOmega }\).

Industry observers note that to conclude, we have established a versatile analogue simulator for self-interacting relativistic quantum fields with a tunable mass in 2 + 1 dimensions, and observed non-perturbative phenomena that point the way to many future studies. The damping of the global ϕ oscillations, accompanied by an emergence of spatial structures (k > 0 excitations), is expected to be analogous to cosmological preheating and reheating11,12. The π phase jump that places the field at the top of the sine-Gordon potential initiates dynamics associated with a quench through a discrete symmetry-breaking phase transition (with the energy minima changing from ϕ = π to ϕ = 0 and 2π). Generalizing the π phase jump to a ramp of Ω from a positive to a negative value, one can study the associated Kibble–Zurek mechanism50, linked to the formation of topological defects such as cosmic strings and domain walls13,14. Studies of domain-wall networks could provide insights into cosmological dark-matter production in axion scenarios51,52 and gravitational-wave signals in a broad family of particle-physics models53. In this context, a particularly interesting possibility is to use vector light shifts to deterministically imprint specific initial domain-wall configurations and study their subsequent dynamics, including their relaxation and decay54,55. Finally, using Floquet engineering to stabilize the system at ϕ = π would enable studies of false-vacuum decay15,16,41,42 in a relativistic, cosmologically relevant setting17,18,19.

Industry observers note that our experiments were performed in a uniform two-dimensional optical box trap formed by repulsive 532-nm light. The two-dimensional confinement was provided by an accordion lattice with trapping frequency ωz/(2π) ≈ 1 kHz, generated holographically56 with a digital micro-mirror device. The in-plane confinement was provided by a square box directly projected from another digital micro-mirror device through a high-resolution microscope (numerical aperture 0.7). The box size was approximately 50 μm × 50 μm for Fig. 1c, and 30 μm × 30 μm for the rest of the experiments.

It has been revealed that the radio-frequency field that couples the two hyperfine states was derived from a vector signal generator (Keysight N5172B). Using in-phase and quadrature modulation, we independently and simultaneously controlled the amplitude, phase and frequency of the radio-frequency field; to prevent carrier feed-through from contaminating the signal, we used a 200-kHz baseband offset. This allowed us to dynamically attenuate the radio-frequency power by >60 dB, and realize Ω/(2π) ≲ 10Hz while retaining the ability to perform fast π/2 rotation at Ω/(2π) > 10kHz. The calibration error for Ω was ≲1% (standard deviation).

According to recent reports, to stabilize the magnetic field B, we first regulated the current through our coils using a feedback loop with a bandwidth >1 kHz and then cancelled the residual 50-Hz mains oscillations using feedforward. This cancelled most of the high-frequency noise from the power supply. To counter slow thermal drifts, we periodically (approximately once per minute) calibrated the field using partial Landau–Zener transfers. On the basis of Zerr from the calibration data, we estimated the residual field variations to be about 150 μG (root mean square).

The two-dimensional interaction parameters are given by \({g}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}=\)\(({\hbar }^{2}/m)\sqrt{8{\rm{\pi }}}\,{a}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}/{{\ell }}_{z}\), where \({a}_{\sigma {\sigma }^{{\prime} }}\) are the s-wave scattering lengths, which we calculate using coupled-channel calculations57,58, and \({{\ell }}_{z}=\sqrt{\hbar /(m{\omega }_{z})}\) (ref. 47).

where \({g}_{{\rm{d}}}=({g}_{\uparrow \uparrow }{g}_{\downarrow \downarrow }-{g}_{\uparrow \downarrow }^{2})/({g}_{\uparrow \uparrow }+{g}_{\downarrow \downarrow }-2{g}_{\uparrow \downarrow })\), κ = (g↑↑ + g↓↓ − 2g↑↓)/4, and Z0 = − Δ/κ, with Δ = (g↑↑ − g↓↓)/4.

The two relevant interaction-energy scales are then μd = gdn for the density degrees of freedom (which for Z = Z0 reduces to the standard density chemical potential) and μs = κn for the spin degrees of freedom.

For Ω ≫ μs/ħ and δ = 0, the plasma frequencies for oscillations near ϕ = 0 and ϕ = π are \({\omega }_{{\rm{p}},0}=\sqrt{\varOmega (\varOmega +2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/\hbar )}\) and \({\omega }_{{\rm{p}},{\rm{\pi }}}=\sqrt{\varOmega (\varOmega -2{\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}/\hbar )}\). By measuring ωp,0 − ωp,π ≈ 2μs/ħ, we calibrate μs and hence n. We summarize the interaction parameters relevant for our experiments in Extended Data Table 1.

In the main text we give the simpler and more intuitive approximate equations that assume Z0 = 0. For all expressions in the main text other than equations (2) and (3), for which the exact forms can be obtained from equations (9) and (11), the corrections due to non-zero Z0 can be incorporated by simply replacing Ω by Ω′ and μs by \({\mu }_{{\rm{s}}}^{{\prime} }\). For our experiments, these corrections are usually negligible (compared with the statistical errors), as we illustrate in Fig. 3c by plotting both the predictions that take into account the Z0 corrections (dotted lines) and the approximate predictions that assume Z0 = 0 (solid lines). For Figs. 4 and 5, the corrections are similarly negligible and for simplicity we ignore them, using only the simpler theory given in the main text. The only perceptible correction, which we do include when comparing the data with theory, is in Fig. 6, where, for Z0 = 0.53, the expected wall width \(w=\sqrt{\hbar /(2m{\varOmega }^{{\prime} })}\) is approximately 8% smaller than \(\sqrt{\hbar /(2m\varOmega )}\).

In a recent development, in Extended Data Fig. 1, we also examine the range of k values for which the dispersion of our spin modes, ωs(k) in equation (5), mimics well the relativistic dispersion ωr(k) in equation (6). As long as k < 1/ξs, the difference between ωs and ωr is ≲20% even for Ω = 0, and it reduces with increasing Ω.

Industry observers note that most importantly, the domain walls we observe in Figs. 5 and 6 are deep in the long-wavelength, relativistic regime. For these walls, the relevant k modes are k ≲ 1/w, and even for our largest Ω in Fig. 6, 1/w is still smaller than the smallest 1/ξM (purple dashed line) shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. In this k range, ωs(k) and ωr(k) are essentially identical.

Recent findings suggest that in Extended Data Fig. 2, we illustrate how the large-amplitude plasma oscillations, such as shown in Fig. 5b, damp at long times. This damping is accompanied by emergence of spatial structures corresponding to a transfer of energy from k = 0 to higher-k modes; qualitatively, this is what is expected in models of cosmological preheating and reheating11,12.

It has been revealed that in Extended Data Fig. 3, we create domain walls as in Fig. 5c, and take consecutive images of n+ and n− in the same experimental run, which demonstrates that the two density distributions are complementary.

From our nRB(x, y) images, we extract ϕtot = q ⋅ r + ϕ using a convolutional neural network59, trained on synthetic data that mimic the experimental images. The network generates quadrature maps I(x, y) and Q(x, y) that approximate, respectively, \(\cos [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\) and \(\sin [{\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}}(x,y)]\), and we extract ϕtot(x, y) as the phase of I(x, y) + iQ(x, y).

In Extended Data Fig. 4, we illustrate the fidelity of this extraction for two examples shown in Fig. 5d and two additional ones from the same dataset. Left to right, we show: (1) the nRB images, (2) the reconstructed \([1+\cos ({\phi }_{{\rm{tot}}})]/2\), which is essentially the de-noised version of the fringes seen in nRB, (3) the contours tracing the maxima of the reconstructed fringes, (4) the overlaying of these contours on the original images, and (5) the extracted ϕ(x, y).

We obtain ϕ(x, y) from ϕtot(x, y) by subtracting the independently calibrated carrier phase q ⋅ r, but note that, because the relative phase between the Raman–Bragg beams and the radio-frequency coupling is random, our measurement determines ϕ(x, y) only up to a global offset. We fix this offset such that ⟨eiϕ⟩ is real and negative for t = 0 ms (as ϕ is jumped to π), and real and positive for t = 10 ms (appropriate for relaxation to ϕ = 0 (mod 2π), as observed in the n± images).

The data that support the findings of this study are available in the Apollo repository at https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.134394.

Latest Update: Kimi Antonelli makes history as youngest F1 champion

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (358 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.
  • The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.
  • Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kimi Antonelli became Formula One's youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third in the Mexico City Grand Prix behind race winner Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

The previous recordholder was Germany's Sebastian Vettel, who first became a world champion at age 23 in 2010.

Antonelli is also the first Italian champion since 1953.

It has been revealed that "I'm speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened," said Antonelli after finishing the race.

His parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car.

He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

"It's been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max ​and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future," the 20-year-old said.

Antonelli, who secured the title with four races remaining, said the final lap was complicated by the excitement of what he had achieved.

It has been revealed that "I think I lost two seconds because I could not see ahead, I think I saw two Ferraris," he said. "It was very special, a lot of memories went through my mind at that moment, and I let it all out after achieving one of my biggest dreams.".

Antonelli has now risen to 380 points with four races remaining. Verstappen (261) snuck past Hamilton (259) in the standings, but they will be racing for second the rest of the ​way.

Antonelli started the race in ​fourth and needed to finish ‌ninth or better to secure the championship on Sunday no matter what his peers did.

He had a relatively smooth run, though the race was interrupted by a red flag around Lap ​45 when Valtteri Bottas crashed.

Verstappen, meanwhile, claimed his sixth victory at the Mexico City Grand Prix, further cementing his affinity with the circuit.

After Mexico, F1 will head to Brazil and then to Las Vegas.

The final two Grands Prix are scheduled to be held in Qatar and Abu Dhabi. But it remains uncertain whether they will take place, given the geopolitical instability in the region.

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .
  • "Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," noted local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.
  • The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," noted local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.".

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property.".

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, california's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Industry observers note that miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the fresh ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," remarked Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

It has been revealed that even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

Industry observers note that california's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging prepares or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

It has been revealed that but those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

Industry observers note that A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is indicates both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air.".

Monza star Varela has already attracted interest from several clubs around Europe. The latest report from Corriere dello Sport claims that Premier League sides Tottenham, Brentford and Sunderland have already sounded out the striker’s availability, while Liverpool regularly send scouts to watch him.

Varela is a upcoming Monza signing, joining the newly promoted Serie A side over the summer on a €2.5m deal from Benfica.

The 21-year-old has scored nine goals in ten Serie A games so far this season, resulting in the best scorer in Italy’s top flight.

Other European clubs, including Juventus, Napoli and Arsenal, have recently been linked with a January move for the Portuguese striker, who has recently received his first senior call-up with his national team.

His former club Benfica do not have an option to re-sign him, but only retain a 20% sell-on clause and can match any offer Monza receive in the coming years.

According to multilpe sources, Monza’s asking price for Varela is €40m.

#48553. Inside Newcastle United's transfer tension: Matthias Jassle wants greater control as he eyes a new No 10 and No 9 in January - but the next four fixtures could make or break him and the club's season, writes CRAIG HOPE

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Inside Newcastle United's transfer tension: Matthias Jassle wants greater control as he eyes a new No 10 and No 9 in January - but the next four fixtures could make or break him and the club's season, writes CRAIG HOPE

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 13:53 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes.
  • In a recent development, the need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 13:53 EST, 19 November 2026.

This time, Matthias Jaissle wants his fingerprints on the bank notes. But what the head coach wishes for in January, and what Newcastle United are willing and able to give, is likely to be very different. When that happens, it rarely ends well - on the pitch or off it.

In a recent development, the need for reinforcement is clear, even on the back of £270million invested in the summer. Jaissle knows as much and is not afraid to say so. The rookie German has to protect himself as much as he does his club.

Because, as Newcastle prepare for what threatens to be a long and testing winter, Jaissle is revisiting the brochure presented to him in the summer. And that is the 38-year-old's concern and frustration - the prospectus for the season ahead was not of his making.

Sources indicate that he arrived three weeks before the start of the campaign and with four of eight signings already through the door. At a cost of £110m, that quartet have started just three Premier League games between them, and each of those by teenager Sean Steur. Baz Toure and Aladji Bamba are virtual spectators, while reserve keeper Ewen Jaouen is injured.

For Jaissle, you suspect, that money was not spent as he would have advised, had he been in situ. Now, in the upcoming year, he wants greater control, as well as a No 10 and No 9. For any Newcastle follower averse to tension, you best watch this transfer window through your fingertips.

Jaissle, sporting director Ross Wilson and chief executive David Hopkinson are the protagonists who will navigate January. At least, that is, if Jaissle makes it into 2027. He deserves that time - not least because of the turbulent and transitional situation he inherited - but the next four fixtures will potentially make or break him and the season.

Head coach Matthias Jaissle is seeking greater control of Newcastle United's transfer strategy.

Aladji Bamba has been a virtual spectator and joined in the summer before Jaissle's arrival.

After the visit of league leaders Arsenal on Saturday, there is a trip to second-placed Brighton, followed by a seismic home double header in the space of five days against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United and bitter rivals Sunderland.

It is why, despite rumblings behind the scenes in recent days of potential transfer discord, Jaissle was on message - the collective, club message - when I asked him about the profile of player he might want in January.

Recent findings suggest that 'It's not the time to talk about the transfer window,' he stated. 'We have players capable to deliver higher performances on the pitch. We have big quality, not only up front, but throughout the whole squad. We believe we can do better and this is what we now want to influence.'.

Industry observers note that however, there was a softening when I sympathised with the head coach over him being judged by a window for which he did not have ownership. Did he, then, want more influence this time?

'Now, it's a different story (compared to the summer), if you're already in and also if you have clarified your clear idea, your clear needs, it's going to be easier,' he mentioned.

'But the transfer market is still a long time ahead, at least it feels like that right now with our fixtures. Our task, especially from my stance, is to focus on the next match and the upcoming challenges.'.

In a recent development, jaissle knows that his case will only be strengthened by a steadying of results, even though, conversely, more defeats would heighten the need for signings. They have lost four from six in all competitions.

The problem is that the hierarchy are on the record as stating the summer business went pretty much exactly as they wished and believed they had a squad for the entire season. There are also Squad Cost Ratio limitations. It is understood there is headroom for one player, but not the two the manager would prefer and not at a fee approaching the £51m they paid for Matias Fernandez-Pardo on deadline day.

Jaissle wants a latest No 9 to compete with the likes of Yoane Wisse who has one league goal.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo (left) has failed to impress so far at Newcastle after his £51m arrival.

The 21-year-old forward is another problem. He is still to score from seven appearances and there is a fear he is not yet strong enough for the Premier League. Interestingly, Jaissle revealed on Thursday his dismay that he was booked during the 1-1 draw at Fulham last time out for screaming at Fernandez-Pardo to stand up.

According to recent reports, that is not to say Jaissle does not believe in the talent of those brought in. He does. But for a coach in his first season in a major European league, he needs players who can impact today, not tomorrow. He needs, and wants, more experience. One of his first recommendations in August was to sign 31-year-old midfielder Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg. Nico Gonzalez eventually arrived in that position, but the 24-year-old looks like a player who has spent two seasons in reserve at Manchester City.

So, it is easy to see why Jaissle needs and wants more in January. It is also easy to see why he might not get it. There could be trouble ahead, and that is not just the upcoming matches.
